text: Suppose you have a scatter of points, each one a house, with its floor area along the bottom and its price up the side. The points rise roughly together, so it is tempting to draw a straight line through them and use it to price the next house. But no straight line passes through every point, which raises the real question of this lesson: among all the lines you could draw, which one is best, and how do we find it without guessing?

A line is described by two numbers, a slope w and an intercept b, and for each house it makes a prediction, w times the area plus b. The vertical gap between a point and the line is called a residual, the part of the price that the line fails to explain. We score a line by squaring every residual and adding them up. Picture each point tied to the line by a spring: the energy stored in a spring grows with the square of its stretch, and the best line is where the springs settle with the least total energy.

Now comes a change of viewpoint that turns this into geometry. Stack all the prices into a single vector y, with one entry per house, so that y becomes one point in a space with as many axes as there are houses. Every choice of slope and intercept also produces a vector, the list of predictions, and those prediction vectors are all combinations of just two columns: the column of areas, and a column of ones. So every prediction a line can ever make lives on one flat plane inside that big space, the span you met in the linear algebra module.

The price vector usually sits off that plane, because real prices are noisy. The best prediction is the point on the plane closest to y, and the closest point is found by dropping a perpendicular, just as a shadow falls straight down when the sun is directly overhead. That shadow is called the projection of y onto the plane, and the leftover arrow, from the shadow up to y, is the residual vector. Minimising the sum of squared residuals is the same as making this arrow as short as possible, which is why least squares and projection are one idea.

Perpendicular has a precise meaning here: the residual has zero dot product with every column that spans the plane. Collect those columns into a matrix X, and the condition reads X transpose times the residual equals zero. Writing the residual as y minus X w and rearranging gives the normal equations, X transpose X, times w, equals X transpose y, where normal is simply the old word for perpendicular. Solving that small system hands us the best weights directly, with no searching at all.

This is the closed-form formula you may have typed before, and now you can see why it works. In code we rarely invert X transpose X ourselves, because inversion magnifies rounding errors when two columns are nearly parallel; instead we hand the problem to a least squares solver, such as NumPy's lstsq, which finds the same projection more safely. The geometry also gives you a check on your work: once the fit is right, the residuals are perpendicular to every feature column, and because the column of ones is among them, the residuals also add up to zero.

Language models lean on this idea too. When researchers want to know whether a model's hidden vectors encode some property, such as the year a sentence is talking about, they fit a simple linear model on those vectors and see how well it predicts, a technique called a linear probe. Next, we keep the straight line but bend its output into a probability, which gives us logistic regression.
